claims.statement: A small group of Chinese characters began as pictures of the thing they name, and the picture is still visible in the modern form: 日 sun, 月 moon, 山 mountain, 水 water, 木 tree. Xu Shen's Shuowen jiezi (c. 100 CE) calls this class xiangxing, 'illustration of a shape'. Most Chinese characters are NOT pictures; the pictographs are the minority and the writing system is a system of word-signs.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Chinese writing: Characteristics (pictographs, ideographs, phonetics)
ChinaKnowledge.de (Ulrich Theobald) — Origin and Types of Chinese Characters; The Chinese Script
Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine — Chinese Writing

claims.statement: Chinese characters are written in a fixed stroke order taught in schools. Among the basic rules: left before right; top before bottom; when a horizontal and a vertical stroke cross, the horizontal is written first (十, 干, 士); enclosing frames are written before their contents and closed last (日, 田, 回).

sources.ref: Ministry of Education, R.O.C. (Taiwan) — Learning Program for Stroke of Chinese Characters, Basic Rules of Stroke Order

Frontiers in Psychology — Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners (states the basic rule set and cites State Language Commission 2020 standard)

claims.statement: In the classical Chinese five-phase (wuxing) correlative scheme the four compass directions plus the centre each carry a colour: east green, south red, centre yellow, west white, north black. The scheme reached its received form in the Han period.

sources.ref: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (peer-reviewed) — Wuxing (Wu-hsing)
Encyclopaedia Britannica — Wuxing (Five Elements): correlation with cardinal directions, seasons and colours

claims.statement: In the Huainanzi the sky cracks and Nüwa melts stones of five colours to patch it, props the four corners with the legs of a turtle, and dams the flood with reed ash.

sources.ref: ChinaKnowledge.de (Ulrich Theobald) — Nü Wa 女媧
Journal of Chinese Humanities (Brill) 3:1 (2017) — A New Model in the Study of Chinese Mythology

claims.statement: The East Asian calendar runs a twelve-year animal cycle in the fixed order rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog, pig. The order was established by the Han period and repeats every twelve years, so any year can be paired with its animal by counting on in twelves.

sources.ref: Victoria and Albert Museum — The lunar zodiac (order of the twelve animals; repeats every 12 years; traced to at least the Han dynasty)
The Metropolitan Museum of Art — Celebrating the Year of the Ox / Year of the Rat exhibition pages (conventional order established by the Eastern Han)

claims.statement: One class of Chinese characters, called huiyi in the Shuowen jiezi's six-category scheme, is built by joining two characters whose meanings combine: 日 sun + 月 moon = 明 bright; 木 tree + 木 tree = 林 grove; 人 person + 木 tree = 休 rest; 女 woman + 子 child = 好 good.

sources.ref: ChinaKnowledge.de (Ulrich Theobald) — Origin and Types of Chinese Characters (huiyi 'combined meaning'; six types after Xu Shen)
Encyclopaedia Britannica — Shuowen jiezi (Xu Shen, c. 100 CE; the six categories of character formation)
Galambos, Imre — Popular character forms (suzi) and semantic compound (huiyi) characters in medieval Chinese manuscripts

claims.statement: The Shanhaijing records that the giant Kua Fu raced the sun, drank a great river dry and set out for the Great Marsh but did not reach it; the staff he dropped grew into a forest of peach trees. The account is transmitted in the 'Classic of the Great Wilderness: North'.

sources.ref: Journal of Chinese Humanities (Brill) 3:1 (2017) — A New Model in the Study of Chinese Mythology (locates 'Kua Fu Chases the Sun' in the Dahuangbei jing of the Shanhaijing and quotes the passage)
Birrell, Anne — Chinese Mythology: An Introduction (Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993); reviewed in The Journal of Asian Studies (Cambridge)

claims.statement: A Turkic or Mongol felt tent is a round frame of a lattice wall, roof poles and a crown ring, covered with felt and tightened with ropes, and it is built to be dismantled and reassembled. In Kyrgyz and Kazakh usage the lattice wall is the kerege and raising the dome is shanyrak; the Mongol ger's counterpart crown is the toono.

sources.ref: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage — Traditional craftsmanship of the Mongol Ger and its associated customs ('a round structure of walls, poles and a peaked roof covered with canvas and felt, and tightened with ropes')

UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage — Traditional knowledge and skills in making Kyrgyz, Kazakh and Karakalpak yurts (collapsible wooden circular frame; kerege; shanyrak; assembled and dismantled in a short time)
British Museum — yurt components in the ethnographic collection (wall sections, roof struts, ties, door lintel), reg. W.As1973-09 series

claims.statement: The oldest surviving writing in a Turkic language stands on stone monuments in the Orkhon valley in central Mongolia, about 360 km south-west of Ulaanbaatar. The two great stelae were raised in 732 and 735 CE for the prince Kul Tigin and his brother; the script was deciphered by Vilhelm Thomsen in 1893. The valley is a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape and is still grazed by herders.

sources.ref: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape (List no. 1081): central Mongolia, c. 360 km south-west of Ulaanbaatar, 121,967 ha, still grazed by nomadic pastoralists
Encyclopaedia Britannica — Orhon inscriptions (discovered 1889 in the Orhon valley, northern Mongolia; deciphered 1893 by Vilhelm Thomsen; monuments erected 732 and 735 CE)

claims.statement: Old Turkic runiform script is normally written right to left within a line, with successive lines running from bottom to top; some inscriptions instead alternate direction line by line (boustrophedon), in which case the letter shapes are mirrored on the reversed lines. The script is alphabetic and derives from Sogdian, not from Germanic runes, despite the nickname.

sources.ref: The Unicode Standard, Chapter 14 (Central Asian scripts) — Old Turkic: right-to-left within a row, rows running bottom to top; boustrophedon variant with reversed letter shapes
ScriptSource (SIL International) — Old Turkic, Orkhon Runic script detail
ISO/IEC JTC1/SC2/WG2 N3357R2 (L2/08-071) — Proposal to encode the Old Turkic script in the UCS

claims.statement: The Old Turkic letters are built from straight cuts and simple angles because they were made to be carved into hard stone with a chisel; the same constraint shapes the herd marks (tamga) cut on rock and property.

sources.ref: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC2/WG2 N3357R2 (L2/08-071) — Proposal to encode the Old Turkic script in the UCS (letterform repertoire and epigraphic context)

claims.statement: The Book of Dede Korkut tells of Tepegöz, a one-eyed giant of the Oghuz tradition, confronted by the hero Basat; the Odyssey tells of Polyphemus, a one-eyed giant confronted by Odysseus. Scholars have compared the two since the early nineteenth century and the comparison now takes in hundreds of related tales. The two accounts end differently: Basat kills Tepegöz, while Odysseus only blinds Polyphemus and escapes.

sources.ref: d'Huy, Julien — Polyphemus (Aa. Th. 1137): a phylogenetic reconstruction of a prehistoric tale, Nouvelle Mythologie Comparée / New Comparative Mythology 1 (2013), 3–18
Motif Akademi Halkbilimi Dergisi (DergiPark, peer-reviewed) — comparative study of Basat and Odysseus in the Tepegöz narratives

claims.statement: Persian is written in the Arabic script from right to left, but numbers inside the same line run left to right, so a Persian line is genuinely bidirectional.

sources.ref: W3C — Text Layout Requirements for the Arabic Script (alreq): right-to-left script with left-to-right digits, i.e. bidirectional text
Unicode Standard Annex #9 — Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (digit categories EN and AN; reordering of numbers within right-to-left runs)

claims.statement: A letter of the Perso-Arabic script takes up to four shapes according to its place in a word: isolated, initial, medial and final. A small set of letters has only isolated and final shapes and therefore does not join to the letter that follows it, which breaks the word into pieces.

sources.ref: W3C — Arabic & Persian Layout Requirements (four positional forms defined as isolated, initial, medial, final; conditional joining)
The Unicode Standard, Chapter 9 (Middle Eastern scripts) — Arabic: contextual shaping and non-joining letters
Kew, Jonathan (SIL International) — Notes on some Unicode Arabic characters: recommendations for usage

claims.statement: The Alborz range runs along the southern shore of the Caspian Sea and separates a dry plateau from a wet coast: the Caspian slopes carry humid Hyrcanian forest with over 1,000 mm of rain a year in Gilan, while the southern slopes share the arid climate of the Iranian plateau. Mount Damavand, about 5,600 m, is the highest peak in Iran and stands in the central Alborz.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Alborz Mountains (separates the wetter Caspian lowlands from the deserts of central Iran; over 40 inches of precipitation in Gilan)
NASA Earth Observatory — Snowcapped Mount Damavand (highest mountain in Iran, c. 5,600 m; part of the Alborz range bordering the Caspian)
Alpine Botany (Springer) — A bioclimatic characterization of high elevation habitats in the Alborz mountains of Iran (500–1500 mm on northern slopes; Hyrcanian forest to c. 2400 m)

claims.statement: The Persian chaharbagh is a walled garden quartered by two crossing water channels; the type is named in Persian sources from the eleventh century onward. The English word paradise descends from Old Iranian pairidaeza, 'walled around', by way of Greek paradeisos and Latin paradisus.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Iranica — ČAHĀRBĀḠ (garden divided into four quarters by two cross-axial water courses; attested from the fifth/eleventh century)
Encyclopaedia Iranica — GARDEN v. Achaemenid period (Avestan pairidaēza-, Old Persian *paridaida-, into Greek paradeisoi and Latin paradisus)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre — The Persian Garden (List no. 1372): geometric layout, water channels and basins dividing the enclosed space into quarters

claims.statement: Four separate traditions each name a great bird: the Simorgh in Persian tradition, where in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh she raises the abandoned child Zal in her nest in the Alborz; the fenghuang in China; the ho-o in Japan, a Japanese form of the fenghuang; and the bennu in Egypt, shown as a grey heron and tied to the morning sun.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Iranica — ZĀL (Sam abandons the white-haired infant in the Alborz; the Simorgh takes him to her nest and rears him; Sam later recovers him)
Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge — The Shahnameh: a Persian Cultural Emblem, object records 'The Simorgh restores Zal to Sam'
Encyclopaedia Britannica — fenghuang; ho-o bird; phoenix (bennu as a grey heron tied to the morning sun and the creation)
The Metropolitan Museum of Art — 'Zal in the Simurgh's Nest', folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings)

claims.statement: The Ganga rises from the Gangotri Glacier in the Himalayas of Uttarakhand, runs about 2,510 km south-east past Haridwar, Prayagraj, Varanasi and Patna, crosses into Bangladesh, joins the Brahmaputra and the Meghna and reaches the Bay of Bengal through a delta shared by two countries.

claims.statement: Five great South Asian rivers begin at five named places: the Ganga at the Gangotri Glacier, the Yamuna at the Yamunotri Glacier, the Brahmaputra at the Chemayungdung Glacier in south-western Tibet, the Indus on the northern flank of the Kailash Range, and the Sutlej at Lake La'nga in south-western Tibet, above 4,600 m. FOUR of the five begin in ice; the Sutlej begins in a lake.

claims.statement: Vietnamese is written in the Latin-based quoc ngu alphabet and carries six tones on the vowel. Five tones take a written mark - grave, acute, hook above, tilde and dot below - and the sixth is written with no mark at all. The mark changes the word: ma, ma with grave, ma with acute, ma with hook, ma with tilde and ma with dot below are six different words.

sources.ref: The Unicode Standard, Chapter 7 (Europe-I, Modern and Liturgical Scripts) — the five combining marks used for Vietnamese tone (U+0300 grave, U+0309 hook above, U+0303 tilde, U+0301 acute, U+0323 dot below)

claims.statement: A dragon boat is long and narrow, from about 12 m upward, carries a carved dragon head at the prow and a tail at the stern, is steered from the stern and is paddled in two rows in time to a drummer who sits at the bow. The dragon boat festival is on UNESCO's Representative List and is kept in Vietnam as well as in China.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Dragon Boat Festival (boats narrow and long, 40 ft to more than 100 ft, dragon head and tail, steerer at the stern, two rows of paddlers, drummer at the bow)
UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage — Dragon Boat festival (Representative List, 2009)

claims.statement: The Red River delta in northern Vietnam is a flat triangle of about 7,000 square kilometres reaching some 150 km inland and 80 km along the coast, with Hanoi standing on it. Because the delta is flat, flood water spreads sideways instead of running away, and the delta has been protected by an earth dyke system built and rebuilt over roughly two thousand years.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Red River delta (flat triangular region, c. 2,700 sq mi / 7,000 sq km, extending c. 150 km inland and 80 km along the coast; Hanoi and Haiphong)
Springer — The Evolution of Water Management in the Red River Delta of Vietnam and a Case of Chuc Son, Hanoi City (dyke building tradition over more than 2000 years)
sources.locator: Springer · Cham 2021 · in: Water Management in the Red River Delta, ch. 19

sources.ref: International Journal of Asian Studies (Cambridge) — Constrained river, constrained choices: seasonal floods and colonial authority in the Red River Delta

claims.statement: One of the earliest recorded Vietnamese legends sets a mountain spirit against a water spirit as rivals for a princess. The mountain spirit wins her; the water spirit, having lost, sends heavy rains every year in an effort to defeat him. The story is carried in the fifteenth-century collection Linh Nam chich quai, and the mountain figure is honoured in Vietnamese folk tradition as a protector against flood.
